newsitem.title: UK: New Conservative chief Hague stuns with first move.
newsitem.headline: New Conservative chief Hague stuns with first move.

text.p: Britain's new Conservative leader, William Hague, began the task of rebuilding his party on Friday with the shock appointment of veteran politician Cecil Parkinson as party chairman.

A day after defeating former finance minister Kenneth Clarke in a final ballot for the leadership, Hague announced Parkinson, a potent symbol of the Conservative glory days of the 1980s, had accepted a post crucial to rebuilding the party's grass roots support.
After presenting Parkinson, 65, to applauding workers at the party's London headquarters, Hague said: "He is going to be taking on this role to put the party into new fighting shape."
"I think he will combine the youth of the new leadership with the experience of politics for many years and bring great heart to the Conservative party across the country."
The appointment of Lord Parkinson, a close ally of former prime minister Margaret Thatcher, was seen as guaranteeing a strong right-wing flavour in the party's new leadership.

Hague, 36, dismissed suggestions this would hinder his attempts to reinstate party unity. "All parts of the party are working together as will be seen in the shadow cabinet that I will announce in due course."

Parkinson, who admitted he was astonished when approached by Hague, made clear his appointment as party chairman was only for two years while he helped rebuild Conservative support following its landslide defeat by Tony Blair's Labour on May 1.
Parkinson was party chairman more than 14 years ago, playing a key role in Thatcher's 1983 election victory.
But just months later he quit Thatcher's cabinet in a blaze of publicity after making his secretary pregnant. He returned to the cabinet four years later but the scandal dogged him.
Each time his name surfaced, popular newspapers resurrected the scandal with interviews with Sara Keays, who lives in a country cottage with their epileptic child.
Aides to Hague dismissed suggestions by reporters the scandal was likely to return to haunt Parkinson and harm a party which prides itself on its family values.

Instead, they insisted, people should focus on the "perfect partnership" between the party's youngest leader in more than 200 years and one of its most seasoned politicians, made a Lord in 1992 after retiring from the House of Commons.
Labour, delighted Hague beat the experienced Clarke for the leadership of the 164 remaining Conservative MPs -- less than half their 1992 tally -- said he had made his first mistake.

"He's fallen at the first hurdle and shown he is a prisoner of the right by appointing Mrs Thatcher's chairman from 15 years ago. There could not be a better example of a mistaken fresh start," said a Labour party spokesman.
Hague was due to continue naming people to his team to "shadow" Labour's cabinet later on Friday and over the weekend.

He was expected to select some of his former rivals in the leadership race to show he was serious about wanting to heal the party's wounds. But one and possibly two key names will be missing, spelling potential trouble.
Former finance minister Clarke announced on Thursday he was stepping down from the political front line after 26 years.

Few commentators also see room in the new team for staunch anti-European John Redwood, whose backing of Clarke on the eve of the final ballot was seen as a coldly calculated marriage of opposites driven only by a desire to stop Hague.
